attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. He credits followers for help with the count, but he states and endorses the count himself.

semantics.note: Faithfully keeps 'at least ten' and the either/or failure: not matching the prompt, or not matching real-world expectations. It drops 'many subtle', which doesn't affect the count.

contract.note: The counting rules are reasonable: distinct defects, allowance for the fantasy unicorn premise, and artistic choices counted only with justification. Because Marcus gave no rule for when one defect counts as several, the result depends on the evaluator's counting choices.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no evidence items. Neither the image nor the full prompt could be retrieved, and no independent audit was found. Marcus's own answer key can't confirm itself. Nothing establishes ten distinct discrepancies or fewer, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence, offered as the first of his 'three morals'.

semantics.note: A general observation that the drafter's wording paraphrases faithfully, with no added scope. Reading it as a general tendency rather than a universal rule is appropriate.

contract.note: The plain reading (a capability gap: convincing appearance is achieved more reliably than detailed consistency) is the ordinary contextual sense. Choosing Jan 2023 to Jan 2024 as the window is the evaluator's choice, but a reasonable one. Excluding cost and effort is fair.

evidence.note: T2I-CompBench (July 2023), within the window. The quoted passage is about coarse metrics missing fine-grained binding and spatial errors. It indirectly supports a gap between apparent and actual prompt adherence.

GenEval (Oct 2023), within the window and checked against human judgments. The best tested models got only 15% of relative-position images and 35% of attribute-binding images right. Only open-source models were tested.

reviews.rationale: Two benchmark studies from the period document systematic failures on detailed prompt requirements (spatial relations, attribute binding), even where coarse image-text similarity looks fine. That fits the claimed gap. The packet has no counterevidence. One limit: the excerpts measure visual appearance only indirectly.

attribution.note: Marcus's own explanatory sentence in the post.

semantics.note: A causal claim about where hallucinations come from, and the paraphrase is faithful. The 'tiny bits' wording is metaphorical, and Marcus doesn't say whether he means the full cause or one contributing cause.

contract.note: Reading the metaphor as statistical generation without verification is fair. The result depends on that reading, and on whether he meant a full or a partial cause; Marcus supplied neither.

evidence.note: Chain-of-Verification (Sept 2023): adding verification reduces hallucinations but doesn't remove them. That backs the importance of checking, but it doesn't test where errors come from.

Kalai and Vempala (Nov 2023) give a statistical account of hallucination under stated assumptions. It neither confirms nor rejects the fragment-and-reconstruct explanation or the missing-checker explanation.

reviews.rationale: No item in the packet tests the full proposed mechanism with controlled comparisons. Verification studies show checking reduces errors without explaining why errors arise. The statistical account is compatible with Marcus's explanation without confirming it. The evidence doesn't settle the causal claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own explanatory sentence in the post.

semantics.note: A causal claim about where near-plagiarism comes from. The drafter writes 'without any mechanism', which slightly sharpens Marcus's 'a mechanism like an originality-assessor', but the meaning is essentially kept.

contract.note: Reading 'reconstructing bits' as metaphor and splitting the claim into a copying mechanism plus the absence of an originality check is fair. Because the speaker set no similarity threshold or scope, the evaluator's reading determines the result.

evidence.note: Carlini et al. (Jan 2023) show diffusion models memorize and reproduce training images. This supports only the copying part of the claim, not the role of a missing originality check.
Somepalli et al. (May 2023) find that caption conditioning and duplication in training data affect copying. This qualifies the explanation but doesn't isolate the effect of an originality assessor.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows generators can reproduce training material, which backs part of the claim. No study compares otherwise similar systems with and without an originality check, and other factors (duplication, conditioning) also matter. The full causal claim isn't settled.
